source: Baltic Exchange route definitions (weekly report via DCN, 20 March 2026); EIA World Oil Transit Chokepoints (June 2024); Lloyd's Market Association Joint War Committee (JWLA-033).

chokepoints.name: Strait of Hormuz
chokepoints.flow: 20.9 million barrels of oil a day in 2023: more than a quarter of seaborne oil trade and about a fifth of world oil consumption (EIA). Most goes to Asia. Qatar's LNG exports also pass here.
chokepoints.note: The only sea exit from the Persian Gulf. Deep and wide enough for the largest tankers, with separate inbound and outbound lanes.
chokepoints.bypass: No sea detour. Saudi Arabia's East–West pipeline to Yanbu on the Red Sea (5 million b/d) and the UAE pipeline to Fujairah (1.5 million b/d) can carry part of the oil; EIA estimated about 2.6 million b/d of spare pipeline capacity.
chokepoints.insurance: A Joint War Committee listed area. In March 2026 (JWLA-033) London insurers extended the listed areas to Bahrain, Djibouti, Kuwait, Oman and Qatar. In July 2026, war-risk quotes for a Hormuz transit were reported at 2–6% of hull value (Insurance Business, citing Marsh).

chokepoints.name: Bab el-Mandeb
chokepoints.flow: 8.6 million barrels of oil a day in 2023 (EIA). Together with Suez and the SUMED pipeline, about 11% of seaborne oil trade, plus most Asia–Europe container trade.
chokepoints.note: The southern gate of the Red Sea, between Yemen and Djibouti. Houthi attacks on ships from late 2023 made most container lines and many tankers sail around Africa instead.
chokepoints.bypass: Around the Cape of Good Hope. For Asia–North Europe this adds roughly 3,000–3,500 nautical miles and 10–14 days.
chokepoints.insurance: Part of the Joint War Committee listed areas (southern Red Sea and Gulf of Aden), so every transit needs an additional war-risk premium, and some owners and crews refuse it.

chokepoints.name: Suez Canal
chokepoints.flow: 8.8 million barrels of oil a day in 2023 including the SUMED pipeline (EIA). Asia–Europe container and car-carrier trade depends on it.
chokepoints.note: A sea-level canal without locks, about 190 km long. The canal authority charges transit dues based on the ship's Suez Canal tonnage; 'Suezmax' is the largest tanker that can pass fully laden.
chokepoints.bypass: The SUMED pipeline (2.5 million b/d) carries crude from the Red Sea to the Mediterranean. Otherwise around the Cape of Good Hope.
chokepoints.insurance: Groundings and blockages here are hull and P&I events; the 2021 Ever Given grounding blocked the canal for six days and led to a large general average and salvage claim.

chokepoints.name: Strait of Malacca
chokepoints.flow: 23.7 million barrels of oil a day in 2023, the largest oil chokepoint (EIA), plus most trade between Europe, the Gulf and East Asia.
chokepoints.note: Narrow and shallow in the Singapore Strait, with heavy traffic. 'Malaccamax' is the largest ship that can pass; the deepest-loaded ships use the deeper Lombok and Makassar straits instead.
chokepoints.bypass: Through Indonesia via the Lombok or Sunda straits, which adds distance. A Myanmar–China pipeline carries a small volume of oil.
chokepoints.insurance: High traffic density makes collision and grounding the main risks; piracy incidents are mostly petty theft at anchor.

chokepoints.name: Panama Canal
chokepoints.flow: 2.1 million barrels of oil a day in the year to September 2023, about 3% of seaborne oil (EIA), plus large volumes of US grain, LPG and LNG to Asia and container traffic to the US East Coast.
chokepoints.note: Lock canal fed by fresh water from Gatun Lake. Drought in 2023–24 forced draft limits and fewer transits. The Neopanamax locks (2016) take far bigger ships than the old 'Panamax' size.
chokepoints.bypass: Via the Suez Canal or the Cape of Good Hope, or around South America; the detours can add thousands of miles. A trans-Panama pipeline carries some crude.
chokepoints.insurance: Delays mean demurrage and lost time rather than physical damage; who pays depends on the charter party.

chokepoints.name: Turkish Straits
chokepoints.flow: 3.4 million barrels of oil a day in 2023, slightly more than half crude (EIA), plus grain from Ukraine and Russia.
chokepoints.note: The only sea link between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean. The Bosporus is less than half a nautical mile wide at its narrowest; Türkiye controls traffic under the Montreux Convention.
chokepoints.bypass: No sea alternative for Black Sea ports. The Baku–Tbilisi–Ceyhan pipeline carries Caspian crude around it.
chokepoints.insurance: Black Sea calls carry war-risk premiums because of attacks on ships and ports in the war in Ukraine.

chokepoints.name: Danish Straits
chokepoints.flow: 4.9 million barrels of oil a day in 2023, mostly Russian exports from Baltic ports (EIA).
chokepoints.note: The Great Belt, Little Belt and Øresund connect the Baltic with the North Sea. The deepest route limits draught, so the largest tankers cannot load fully in the Baltic. Many shadow-fleet tankers pass here, close to Norway.
chokepoints.bypass: The Kiel Canal for small ships only.
chokepoints.insurance: Coastal states check insurance documents of tankers passing, a response to uninsured shadow-fleet ships.

chokepoints.name: Cape of Good Hope
chokepoints.flow: About 6 million barrels of oil a day in 2023, about 8% of seaborne oil (EIA), and the main detour when the Red Sea is avoided.
chokepoints.note: Not a chokepoint but the alternative route between the Atlantic and Indian oceans, with rough winter weather. Capesize bulk carriers and VLCCs too big for Suez sail here anyway.
chokepoints.bypass: This is the bypass. EIA estimates that closing Suez and SUMED adds about 15 days from the Arabian Sea to Europe.
chokepoints.insurance: Heavy-weather damage to ships and cargo is a classic hull and cargo claim on this route.

chokepoints.name: Strait of Gibraltar
chokepoints.flow: The Mediterranean's link to the Atlantic, used by all Suez traffic heading to northern Europe and the Americas.
chokepoints.note: About 14 km wide at the narrowest point, with a traffic separation scheme.

chokepoints.name: Dover Strait
chokepoints.flow: One of the busiest shipping lanes in the world, leading to Rotterdam, Antwerp and Hamburg.
chokepoints.note: Ships follow a traffic separation scheme. Ferries crossing the lanes make collision risk a constant issue.

chokepoints.name: Lombok Strait
chokepoints.flow: The deep-water alternative to Malacca for the largest bulk carriers and tankers between Australia, Brazil and China.
chokepoints.note: Deep enough for fully laden VLOCs and VLCCs. Iron ore from Brazil and Western Australia often passes here.
chokepoints.bypass: Malacca or Sunda for smaller ships.

routes.name: Middle East Gulf → China
routes.quote: Worldscale points (WS), a percentage of a published flat rate in USD per tonne for each route. Brokers convert WS to time-charter equivalent (TCE, USD per day) to compare routes.

hormuz.note: Only part of the oil can reach Yanbu on the Red Sea by pipeline; from there the voyage passes Bab el-Mandeb instead of Hormuz.

malacca.note: Via Lombok and Makassar instead of Malacca.

moves: Middle East export volumes and OPEC+ decisions
Tension around Hormuz (risk premium and war-risk insurance)
Ships returning from long-haul Atlantic trades
routes.course: The benchmark route for VLCC earnings and therefore for VLCC values in sale and purchase. Lenders compare TD3C TCE with the ship's cash breakeven. A transit of Hormuz requires additional war-risk cover, and a VLCC's P&I club stands behind any oil pollution claim.

routes.name: West Africa → China
routes.quote: Worldscale points (WS), a percentage of a published flat rate in USD per tonne for each route. Brokers convert WS to time-charter equivalent (TCE, USD per day) to compare routes.
moves: Chinese demand for light sweet crude
Competition from US and Brazilian barrels
routes.course: A long-haul route: about twice the distance of TD3C, so each cargo ties up a VLCC for much longer. More long-haul cargoes mean more ton-miles and tighter VLCC supply.

routes.name: US Gulf → China
routes.quote: Lump sum in USD for the whole voyage, converted to TCE.
moves: The price spread between US WTI and Middle East crude
Chinese trade policy towards US oil
US export terminal capacity (VLCCs often load by lightering offshore)
routes.course: One of the longest crude voyages: a classic ton-mile story. When US crude flows to Asia, VLCC demand rises far more than the export volume alone suggests.

routes.name: West Africa → UK-Continent
routes.quote: Worldscale points (WS), a percentage of a published flat rate in USD per tonne for each route. Brokers convert WS to time-charter equivalent (TCE, USD per day) to compare routes.
moves: Competition from US and Guyana crude (TD27)
routes.course: Suezmax earnings in the Atlantic basin. Shorter voyages mean less ton-mile demand per cargo than the long-haul routes to Asia.

routes.name: US Gulf → UK-Continent
routes.quote: Worldscale points (WS), a percentage of a published flat rate in USD per tonne for each route. Brokers convert WS to time-charter equivalent (TCE, USD per day) to compare routes.
moves: Hurricane season in the Gulf of Mexico
routes.course: US crude replaced Russian barrels in Europe after sanctions, which made this a core Aframax trade.

routes.name: Cross North Sea
routes.quote: Worldscale points (WS), a percentage of a published flat rate in USD per tonne for each route. Brokers convert WS to time-charter equivalent (TCE, USD per day) to compare routes.
moves: North Sea production and field maintenance
routes.course: A short-haul route: port time and weather matter more than sea days. Norwegian and UK crude is priced and shipped on similar terms.

routes.name: Mongstad → Rotterdam (Norwegian crude)
routes.quote: Similar to cross-North Sea routes (TD7): Worldscale points.
moves: Johan Sverdrup and other Norwegian field output
Winter weather in the North Sea
routes.course: Your local export: much of Norway's crude, including Johan Sverdrup, is loaded at Mongstad near Bergen. Short voyages, so port time and weather drive the economics.

routes.name: Middle East Gulf → UK-Continent
routes.quote: Lump sum in USD, converted to TCE.

bab-el-mandeb.note: Around the Cape of Good Hope instead of the Red Sea.

suez.note: Around the Cape of Good Hope instead of Suez.

moves: Europe's diesel and jet imports after it stopped buying Russian products
New export refineries in the Middle East
routes.course: Europe now imports more diesel and jet from the Middle East and India. Long voyages around Africa absorbed many LR2s and lifted clean tanker earnings.

routes.name: Atlantic triangulation (MR)
routes.to: New York, then US Gulf → Rotterdam
routes.quote: Worldscale points per leg; the basket is quoted as TCE.

legs_extra.label: Short ballast to the US Gulf

moves: European diesel imports from the US Gulf
How short the ballast leg is between cargoes
routes.course: Triangulation cuts ballast: the ship carries gasoline west, sails a short way empty, then carries diesel east. Less ballast time per laden day lifts the round-trip TCE, which is why the Baltic publishes it as a basket.

routes.name: West Australia → China
routes.quote: USD per tonne of cargo, converted to TCE. The C5TC index averages five Capesize time-charter routes.
moves: Chinese steel production and iron ore stocks
The share of long-haul Brazilian ore
routes.course: The highest-volume Capesize route but a short one: a round trip takes about a month. Ore miners also own or charter their own ships, which matters for spot demand.

routes.name: Brazil → China
routes.quote: USD per tonne of cargo, converted to TCE.
moves: Vale's export volumes and the Brazilian rainy season
routes.course: About three times the distance of C5 for each tonne. A shift of China's ore buying from Australia to Brazil raises Capesize ton-mile demand even if China imports the same tonnes.

routes.name: Brazil soybeans → China
routes.quote: USD per tonne; Panamax/Kamsarmax earnings are tracked as a time-charter average (P5TC).
moves: The Brazilian harvest (peak shipments in spring)
China's soybean demand for animal feed
US–China trade policy (US soybeans are the alternative)
routes.course: A seasonal long-haul trade. Port congestion in Brazil during the harvest peak also removes ships from the market for weeks.

routes.name: US Gulf grain → China via Panama
routes.quote: USD per tonne.

panama.note: Around the Cape of Good Hope when Panama slots are short.

moves: Panama Canal draft limits and slot auctions
routes.course: The clearest example of a canal decision: wait and pay for a Panama slot, or sail much further via the Cape. Who pays for waiting time depends on the charter party.

routes.name: Indonesia coal → India
routes.quote: USD per tonne or time-charter trips.
routes.course: Short, flexible trips for geared Supramaxes that can load at anchor from barges. These ships switch between many cargoes, so rates move more slowly than Capesize.

routes.name: China → North Europe
routes.quote: USD per 40-foot container (FEU) on the spot market; most volume moves on annual contracts.

bab-el-mandeb.note: Around the Cape of Good Hope, as most container lines have done since early 2024.

suez.note: Around the Cape of Good Hope instead of Suez.

moves: Capacity on the trade (new ships, blank sailings)
routes.course: Container lines run weekly loops, so a longer route needs more ships to keep the same frequency: rerouting via the Cape absorbed a large share of the global fleet. Charter rates for ships from non-operating owners rose with it.

routes.name: China → Mediterranean
routes.quote: USD per FEU (spot).

bab-el-mandeb.note: Around Africa and into the Mediterranean through Gibraltar: the detour is relatively longer than for North Europe.

suez.note: Around Africa and into the Mediterranean through Gibraltar.

moves: Red Sea routing (the Cape detour hits the Mediterranean hardest)
routes.course: Going around Africa adds more for Mediterranean ports than for Rotterdam, because ships must sail back up to Gibraltar. That is why Mediterranean spot rates rose most in the Red Sea crisis.

routes.name: China → US West Coast
routes.quote: USD per FEU (spot).
moves: West Coast port labour and rail links inland
routes.course: The shortest main lane from Asia to the US, sailing a great-circle arc across the North Pacific. Tariff announcements move volumes and rates here first.

routes.name: China → US East Coast via Panama
routes.quote: USD per FEU (spot).

panama.note: Via Suez, the main alternative when Panama is restricted (if the Red Sea is open).

moves: Rail versus all-water routing through the US West Coast
routes.course: Shippers choose between an all-water route via Panama or Suez and the West Coast plus rail. Canal restrictions shift cargo between ports and modes.

routes.name: Qatar LNG → Japan
routes.quote: Mostly long-term charters to the project; spot LNG carrier rates are quoted in USD per day.
moves: Asian gas demand and the JKM price
routes.course: Qatar's LNG fleet is largely on long-term charters backed by the export project: the kind of charter-backed finance banks like. The voyage passes Hormuz, so war-risk cover is part of the cost.

routes.name: Australia → Japan
routes.quote: USD per day (spot TCE).
moves: New ships delivering into the spot market
routes.course: A short Pacific route compared with US cargoes to Asia, so it needs fewer ship-days per cargo.

routes.name: US Gulf → Continent
routes.quote: USD per day (spot TCE).
moves: European gas prices (TTF) against Asian prices (JKM)
routes.course: Since 2022 the US has become Europe's largest LNG supplier, replacing Russian pipeline gas.

routes.name: US Gulf → Japan via Panama
routes.quote: USD per day (spot TCE).

panama.note: Around the Cape of Good Hope, as many US cargoes did during the 2023–24 Panama drought.

moves: The JKM–TTF price spread (Asia versus Europe)
routes.course: Each US cargo to Asia faces a route choice: Panama, Suez or the Cape. Longer routings absorb LNG carriers and support spot rates.

routes.name: Ras Tanura → Chiba (LPG)
routes.quote: USD per tonne, converted to TCE.
routes.course: VLGCs carry propane and butane. Middle East cargoes compete with US cargoes for Asian buyers.

routes.name: Hammerfest LNG → Rotterdam
routes.quote: Mostly contracted volumes; spot cargoes priced against TTF.
moves: Winter weather along the Norwegian coast
routes.course: Norway's only large LNG export plant. A short route to Europe compared with US or Qatari cargoes.
